name: Dermabrasion

lead: Dermabrasion planes down the upper to mid layers of skin so that acne scars and deeper surgical scars end up shallower and smoother once new skin forms. It was the long-standing standard for scar resurfacing before lasers.

A dermatologist or plastic surgeon removes skin layers with a wire brush, diamond wheel or similar tool. Wikipedia says lasers such as CO2 and Er:YAG have largely replaced it, though it remains in use, partly because it may cost less. A claim that it can match or exceed lasers for some conditions rests on a 1998 minipig study.

paras: It is performed under local anaesthesia in a clinical setting, and healing takes roughly 7 to 30 days. It is distinct from microdermabrasion, which is a light, non-invasive exfoliation.
Reported complications include scarring, discoloration, infection, cold-sore reactivation and bleeding. It is an invasive surgical procedure and recovery involves open, healing skin.

angle.text: Dermabrasion sands away the upper skin layers so new, smoother skin forms and acne or surgical scars look shallower. It was the standard scar-resurfacing method before lasers and remains in use. Evidence consists mostly of small trials.

lead: Dermabrasion is a surgical skin-planing procedure in which a dermatologist or plastic surgeon wears away the upper to mid layers of skin, mainly to reduce acne scars and deep surgical scars.[1] It is distinct from microdermabrasion, a lighter non-invasive exfoliation.[1]

Wikipedia states that lasers such as CO2 and Er:YAG have largely replaced it, though dermabrasion remains in use, partly because it may cost less.[1] A claim that it can match or exceed lasers for some conditions rests on a 1998 minipig study cited there.[1]

paras: The procedure usually uses local anaesthesia, often in a surgical suite. Tools described include wire brushes, diamond wheels, sterilised sandpaper and salt crystals; minor bleeding is typical.[1] It is used for deeper acne scars, deep surgical scars, birthmarks, tattoos, sun damage and fine wrinkles.[1]

A review of acne scar pathogenesis, classification and treatment discusses resurfacing among the treatment options.[2] A 1996 study examined a high-energy pulsed CO2 laser for atrophic acne scars, the type of scar for which dermabrasion was previously used.[3] Registered trials include a split-scar trial of dermabrasion in Mohs surgery wounds (29 participants, 2025), a comparison of laser resurfacing and dermabrasion for scar revision (6 participants), a trial comparing microneedling with dermabrasion for early facial scars (recruiting), and a trial of tretinoin versus superficial dermabrasion for stretch marks (32 participants).[4][5][6][7] The sources reviewed here do not summarise their results.
Wikipedia lists scarring, skin discoloration, infection, reactivation of cold sores and bleeding. Lasers are described there as causing little or no bleeding and being less operator-dependent.[1]

A looksmax.org thread asks whether members use derma stamps or dermabrasion for skin or scalp microneedling; one reply describes using a device brand several times a month. The thread is about microneedling tools rather than surgical dermabrasion.[8]
